title: CUDA graph fragmentation and occupancy drift analysis
body:
Summary:

Quick findings from a targeted Nsight timeline sweep on long-lived workloads (100k+ requests, >2 hour runs). We observed a gradual occupancy drop (~6-12%) across some model variants after sustained traffic. The drop correlates with increasing time spent in non-compute work: host-to-device staging, stream synchronization waits, and repeated cudaGraphReplay stalls when graph segments get instantiated repeatedly instead of being reused.

Why this is interesting/impact: 
- Latency drift after warm start: tail latency increases by 10–30 ms on p99 for a subset of GPUs despite stable request QPS.
- Cost: lower sustained occupancy increases time-to-first-byte and overall token cost due to longer kernels.
- Reliability: some jobs hit soft-SLOs after hours of sustained traffic.

What we ran (capture config):
- Target: ded-nd40 instance with A100-SXM4, 8 microbatch workers active.
- Nsight capture: 10-second captures every 15 minutes using nv-nsight-cu-cli --target-processes all --metrics sm__cycles_active.avg,pct,sm__throughput.avg.
- Workload: mix of 4k and 1k context requests (60/40 split) to emulate burst+steady.
- CUDA: cuda 12.2, drivers 535.86, runtime uses cudaGraph API for critical path (replay per-request).

Key observations (timeline + metrics):
1) Fragmented cudaGraph re-instantiation pattern
   - Instead of creating a single long-lived instantiated graph per model shard, the runtime reconstitutes small graph fragments for "prep" (copy, kernel-setup) and then re-invokes instantiate+replay frequently. Nsight shows repeated spikes labeled as "cudaGraphInstantiate" between kernels.
   - Each instantiate introduces CPU-side serialization and device-side context churn; these periods align with increased host-device memcpy times and lower SM utilization immediately after.

2) Stalled kernel launches due to stream interdependencies
   - We see kernels queued on lower-priority streams waiting for small async memcpy on a higher-priority stream (copy for KV cache updates). Timeline heatmap shows idle SM time while memcpy occupies DMA engines.
   - Effective concurrency drops: kernel concurrency drops from 3 concurrent CTAs to 1–2 for short windows.

3) Gradual occupancy drift correlated with memory allocator fragmentation
   - Over long runs, device memory allocator (custom arena) shows increased allocation path length; allocations for temporary scratch buffers move to slightly different addresses leading to poorer coalescing for some kernels (observed in memory access patterns metric).
   - Result: small regressions in warp efficiency and increased global memory transactions.

4) KV cache eviction and rehydration spikes
   - When cache eviction happens (edge cases under bursty traffic), we see a surge of host->device transfers and immediate instantiate/replay calls to rebuild state. This produces short-lived occupancy dips that aggregate into the drift metric.

Small data points (from captures):
- sm__cycles_active.avg: baseline ~84%, after 90m drift -> ~76% on affected kernels.
- sm__warps_active.avg: drops by 8–12% during events.
- Host->device memcpy avg latency for prep region: baseline 0.22 ms -> spikes 1.6 ms when instantiate loop happens.
- Number of cudaGraphInstantiate calls per minute: baseline 0–2 -> observed 18–36 in pathological runs.

Hypotheses (ranking):
A) Excessive instantiate/release of short CUDA graphs causes device-side context work and stalls kernel pipelines.
B) Stream priority inversion from synchronous memcpys used for KV cache updates is throttling DMA and blocking concurrent kernel execution.
C) Memory allocator fragmentation causes degraded memory access patterns for a subset of kernels, magnifying occupancy loss over time.

Immediate mitigations to test (short experiments):
- Switch to persistent instantiated graphs: create/instantiate graphs at model load time, reuse across requests. Measure instantiate call counts and p99 latency. (Experiment PR branch: feature/persistent-cudagraphs)
- Move small KV cache transfers to a dedicated low-priority copy stream with explicit cudaMemcpyAsync + stream semantics to avoid preempting DMA for compute-critical streams.
- Use page-locked (pinned) staging buffers pooled at startup instead of allocating per-request to reduce host->device memcpy jitter.
- Add quick allocator compaction on low-traffic windows (maintain free lists coalesced).

Longer-term mitigations / design changes:
- Rework graph segmentation: combine prep+compute into a single graph where possible to eliminate instantiate/release churn.
- Introduce a streaming policy that assigns KV cache copies to a non-interfering engine (if hardware supports copy engine partitioning).
- Explore persistent kernel strategies (single long-running kernel handling token generation) for high-throughput low-latency slices.
- Improve telemetry: add counters for "cudaGraphInstantiate" counts per instance and per model-version in Console traces.

Open questions / uncertainties:
- Is the allocator fragmentation intrinsic to our pool logic or driven by an upstream third-party library (e.g., fused op library)? Need to instrument allocation stack traces during fragmentation windows.
- How much of observed memcpy jitter is from OS scheduling vs. pinned vs. pageable memory selection?
- Will persistent graphs interact badly with model hot-swapping and rollout policies? Need a canary rollout plan.

Immediate action items (next 2 weeks):
- Ethan: implement instantiate-count telemetry and add a metric to per-model traces (JIRA-ENG-3185).
- Priya: prototype pinned buffer pool and run microbenchmarks using the same Nsight capture cadence.
- Aisha (owner): coordinate a 2-hour soak test with persistent instantiated graphs branch and collect 4 capture points (0m, 30m, 90m, 180m).
- Liam: investigate allocator free-list growth patterns and add a debug build that logs allocation buckets on fragmentation events.

Notes / rough commands used: 
- nsight capture snippet: nv-nsight-cu-cli --metrics "sm__cycles_active.avg.pct,sm__warps_active.avg" --csv --output ./captures/run-$(date +%s).csv --target-processes all --capture-range "duration=10s,period=15m" --trace system,compute,memory
- quick graph debug: insert logging around cudaGraphCreate()/cudaGraphInstantiate()/cudaGraphDestroy() with monotonic timestamps and pointer IDs.

Slack snippets (where I posted captures): #eng-serving-runtime thread "cuda-graph-frag" (see pinned messages)

Appendix: quick checklist for reviewers
- Verify capture tags and time offsets when comparing runs (use host monotonic to align).
- Approve short canary for persistent graphs (needs feature flag gated behind model-version).
- Decide whether to prioritize pinned buffer pool or stream-policy change first; pinned buffers are lower-risk and should be A/B testable.

Unpolished notes / brainstorming (tossed here):
- Could there be NVLink traffic contention if multiple shards share the same host-side staging buffers? Capture inter-GPU memcpy metrics next run.
- Might benefit from holding a tiny pool of persistent cudaStreams per worker pinned to specific copy engines (if PCIe topology allows).
- If instantiate counts correlate strongly with rollout events, tie instantiate suppression to rollout hooks (defer instantiate until after model is fully warmed).

If you review this, please add comments inline or drop notes in the slack thread. I'll upload the recorded nsight captures to the confluence page listed under linked_artifacts for playback.
